# Diagnosing Stuck Windshield Wipers on GM Vehicles

When a vehicle's windshield wipers refuse to return to their parked position and remain frozen in an upright orientation, the issue typically stems from a mechanical disconnect rather than a software glitch. This behavior is particularly prevalent across General Motors platforms, including older models like the 2002 Chevrolet Impala. While online resources often suggest manipulating a specific tab near the wiper transmission, that solution is not universally applicable. If physical inspection reveals no bent tabs, you must look deeper into the actuation mechanism itself to resolve the failure.

The core of the problem lies in how the transmission converts the rotary motion of the motor into the linear movement required for parking. In many GM designs, a small plastic tab or clip located inside the transmission housing is responsible for catching the linkage at the end of the stroke. When this component fails or becomes misaligned, the motor completes its cycle but the linkage does not lock into the "park" position. Consequently, gravity keeps the wiper arms elevated until power is applied again to force them down.

Before attempting invasive repairs, perform a visual inspection of the transmission area accessible under the hood. Locate the wiper motor assembly and remove the cowl panel if necessary to access the linkage arm. Look closely at the connection point between the motor output shaft and the vertical drive rod. On many GM units, there is a distinct plastic tab protruding from the transmission body. This tab must be oriented correctly relative to the drive arm.

If the tab appears straight or unengaged, you may need to manually manipulate it back into its designed position. Using a pair of needle-nose pliers, gently bend the tab inward so that it catches the end of the drive rod when the wiper hits the park position. This action creates a physical stop that overrides any slack in the linkage. Be careful not to apply excessive force; these plastic components are brittle and can snap if over-manipulated. If the tab breaks during this process, you will need to replace the entire transmission unit rather than attempting a field repair.

In cases where the tab is already bent correctly but the wipers still fail to park, the issue likely involves worn bushings or seized linkages within the transmission housing. The internal gears may have stripped, preventing the mechanism from reaching the final travel limit. At this stage, replacing the transmission is often more cost-effective than repairing individual gears.

It is important to distinguish between a mechanical parking failure and a motor control issue. If the wipers move slowly or erratically before stopping, the problem could involve the variable speed resistor or the motor relay, which are separate from the physical tab mechanism. However, when the arms remain rigidly upright immediately after the cycle completes, focus your diagnosis on the linkage catch points.

While this mechanical fix addresses the symptom for many GM owners, it is a temporary measure if the internal wear is severe. Monitor the condition of the plastic tab during future maintenance cycles; repeated bending can eventually lead to fatigue failure. If you encounter resistance while trying to bend the tab, stop immediately and consider sourcing an OEM replacement transmission. Attempting to force a misaligned mechanism can damage the housing, leading to fluid leaks or further disassembly challenges.

For those maintaining older fleet vehicles where parts availability is spotty, documenting the specific configuration of the transmission tab before making adjustments ensures you can reverse-engineer the repair if needed. Always verify that the wiper arms sit flush against the glass in the park position after any adjustment to confirm the mechanical catch is functioning as intended.
